Energy Stores.intro: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. Understanding the different types of energy store is the starting point for all of P1.

sections.title: Types of Energy Store
points: Kinetic — energy of moving objects
Gravitational potential — energy due to height above ground
Elastic potential — energy stored in stretched/compressed objects
Chemical — energy stored in chemical bonds (food, fuel, batteries)
Thermal — energy stored due to temperature (internal energy)
Nuclear — energy stored in atomic nuclei
Electrostatic — energy due to charges
Magnetic — energy in magnetic fields

callout.label: Law of Conservation
callout.text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another. The total energy always stays the same.

keyTerms.def: A way in which energy is held — kinetic, gravitational, thermal, chemical, etc.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores

examTips: Use precise language: 'energy is transferred FROM the chemical store TO the kinetic store' — not just 'energy changes'.
Name both the starting store and the ending store in energy transfer descriptions.
commonMistakes: Saying energy is 'used up' — energy is always conserved, just transferred to less useful stores (e.g. thermal).
Confusing energy stores with energy transfer pathways.

Energy Transfer.intro: Energy is transferred between stores by four pathways: mechanically, electrically, by heating, and by radiation. Understanding these pathways is essential for P1.

sections.title: Transfer Pathways
points: Mechanically — by a force acting over a distance (work done)
Electrically — by an electric current through a circuit
By heating — by conduction, convection or radiation
By radiation — electromagnetic waves (light, infrared, etc.)

sections.title: Energy Diagrams
points: Sankey diagrams show energy transfers — width of arrow proportional to amount
Useful energy goes right; wasted energy (usually thermal) goes down
Energy dissipated = energy spread out into surroundings as thermal energy

sections.title: Reducing Wasted Energy
points: Lubrication — reduces friction → less thermal energy wasted
Insulation — reduces heat loss to surroundings
Streamlining — reduces air resistance

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object: W = F × d (joules)
Diagram showing energy input, useful output and wasted energy
Energy spreading out into surroundings as thermal energy — becomes less useful

examTips: All energy eventually dissipates as thermal energy — it isn't 'lost', just less useful.
In Sankey diagrams: total width in = total width out (conservation of energy).
commonMistakes: Saying wasted energy disappears — it is transferred to the thermal store of surroundings.
Confusing work done (mechanical transfer) with power (rate of energy transfer).

Efficiency.intro: Efficiency measures how well a device transfers energy usefully. No device is 100% efficient — some energy is always wasted.

sections.title: Efficiency Formula

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (× 100 for percentage). Or: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.

points: Efficiency is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%)
No device is 100% efficient — some energy always wasted as heat
More efficient = less energy wasted

sections.title: Improving Efficiency
points: Lubrication — reduces friction in moving parts
Better thermal insulation — reduces heat loss
Regenerative braking in electric cars — captures kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: The fraction of input energy that is transferred to useful output energy
Energy transferred in the desired way by a device
Energy transferred in an unwanted way — usually as thermal energy

examTips: Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal (0.75) or percentage (75%).
Wasted energy = total input − useful output.
An efficiency of 0.75 means 75% of energy is usefully transferred.
commonMistakes: Giving efficiency greater than 1 (or 100%) — this is impossible.
Forgetting to subtract wasted energy: useful = total − wasted.

Specific Heat Capacity.intro: Specific heat capacity (SHC) measures how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Q = mcΔT — where Q = energy (J), m = mass (kg), c = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C), ΔT = temperature change (°C).

sections.title: What SHC Means
points: High SHC = needs lots of energy to heat up (e.g. water = 4200 J/kg°C)
Low SHC = heats up quickly with less energy (e.g. copper = 390 J/kg°C)
Water has a very high SHC — why it is used in cooling systems and is used as a thermal store

keyTerms.def: Energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (J/kg°C)
The energy needed to raise an object's temperature by 1°C

examTips: Q = mcΔT — learn this formula and the units for each quantity.
Water has the highest SHC of common substances — explain why it is used in central heating.
commonMistakes: Using temperature in Kelvin instead of °C for ΔT — the change is the same in either scale.
Forgetting that ΔT = final temperature − initial temperature.

Energy Resources.intro: Energy resources are used to generate electricity and heat. Understanding the advantages and disadvantages of renewable and non-renewable sources is essential for P1.

sections.title: Non-Renewable Resources
points: Fossil fuels: coal, oil, natural gas — burn to produce steam → turbine → generator
Nuclear: uranium fission heats water → steam → turbine
Advantages: reliable, high output, available on demand
Disadvantages: finite (will run out), produce CO₂ (fossil fuels) or radioactive waste (nuclear)

sections.title: Renewable Resources
points: Solar — panels absorb light; PV cells or solar thermal
Wind — turbines turned by wind; no fuel costs
Hydroelectric — falling water drives turbines; reliable
Tidal — tides drive turbines; predictable
Wave — waves move generators; variable
Geothermal — heat from Earth used to make steam
Biomass — burning biological material; considered carbon neutral

callout.label: Key Comparison
callout.text: Non-renewable: reliable but polluting and finite. Renewable: clean and sustainable but often intermittent (not always available on demand).

keyTerms.def: An energy resource that will run out and cannot be replenished
An energy resource that will not run out and is naturally replenished
Device that converts kinetic energy of steam or water into rotational energy
Device that converts rotational kinetic energy into electrical energy

examTips: Most power stations work the same way: fuel heats water → steam → turbine → generator (except solar PV, wind turbines).
Renewable ≠ always available. Wind and solar are intermittent.
Be able to evaluate energy sources for 6-mark questions — consider reliability, cost, environment, land use.
commonMistakes: Saying nuclear is renewable — it uses uranium which is a finite resource.
Saying biomass produces no CO₂ — it does, but the carbon was recently absorbed from the atmosphere.
